title: Disinfectants, Hand Rub, Labels and Selling

say: Disinfectants, Sanitiser, Labelling and Growing the Business. This is module 5, the last module of the course.
These products protect health, so they carry the strictest rules. Let's get them right.

shots.label: Clean first, then rinse
say: Watch this counter being sprayed and wiped with detergent first. Dirt and grease shield germs and use up disinfectant.
So the order is always: clean first, rinse, then disinfect.

shots.label: Gloves and eye protection
say: Before you dilute bleach, put on gloves and eye protection. Use cool water in a ventilated space.

shots.label: Bleach (sodium hypochlorite)

card.title: Grace's bleach dilutions
rows: C1 x V1 = C2 x V2

say: These cups go from strong bleach down to weak dilution. You work it out with C1 times V1 equals C2 times V2.
Grace in Ilorin needed 0.1% for floors and 0.5% for a spill kit. Both took about 286 ml of her 3.5% bleach, just made up to different volumes.
She labels each bucket with strength, date and time, and never tops up an old bucket.

shots.label: Bleach and acid cleaner
shots.banner: Never mix bleach with acid or ammonia
say: Keep these two apart. Never mix bleach with acids, ammonia or other cleaners.
Store diluted bleach in labelled containers, out of sunlight and away from children. Rinse metal surfaces after the contact time.

shots.label: Benzalkonium chloride (BKC)

card.title: Musa's BKC practice sum
card.note: Always follow the real product's label

say: See the surface stay wet while the timer runs. That's contact time, and wiping dry too early is a common failure.
Quats like BKC are inactivated by soap residue, so rinse first. Musa weighed 40 g of 50% concentrate into about 9 litres, then topped up to 10.

shots.label: Registered products only
say: Words like disinfectant or kills 99.9% of germs are health claims. In Nigeria they need NAFDAC registration and efficacy tests.
Until then, sell honestly as cleaners, and teach customers to use registered disinfectants correctly.

shots.label: WHO hand rub, Formulation 1
say: Now the hand rub. These cylinders hold alcohol, hydrogen peroxide and glycerol, the WHO formula.
The peroxide deals with spores, and the glycerol protects skin. Change the formula and it's no longer the WHO formulation.

shots.label: No flames, no generator
say: Methanol is poisonous through the skin and if swallowed. Buy ethanol or isopropyl alcohol with a certificate of analysis.
Alcohol vapour catches fire easily. Mix by an open window with no flames, no cooking gas, no smoking and no generator nearby.

shots.label: Alcoholmeter reading: 90%
say: Hadiza in Sokoto checked her ethanol with an alcoholmeter. It was 90%, not 96%.
So she measured 1,778 ml instead of 1,667 ml, and the finished rub still reached 80%.

shots.label: Fill, close, quarantine
say: Fill, close and label every bottle with the alcohol percentage, batch number, date and Flammable: keep away from fire and flame.
Then hold them for 72 hours before use. The quarantine is part of the formulation.

shots.label: One brand, clear labels
say: Every label needs name, net content, ingredients largest first, directions, cautions, maker, NAFDAC number and batch details.
Ada in Lagos traced a thin bottle to its record in minutes, because of a code like this.
At her desk, Comfort in Asaba added the three layers of cost and divided by 40 bottles.
Packaging was almost as much as the liquid. So she shops for a cheaper pump before raising her price.
Grow in steps, 20 kg, then 50 kg, then 100 kg, testing at each step.

shots.label: Institutional buyers
say: Hotels, schools and offices reorder every month. Ngozi ran a two-week trial, then quoted from real usage.
On 30-day credit she must fund about ₦30,800 of stock each month. Put terms in writing, and never supply unregistered products to clinics.
Now go through the lessons below. Make your dilution chart, your paper hand rub batch, your label set and your cost sheet, then prepare one institutional pitch.
Well done for finishing the course.
